intro: Searching for a criminal barrister near me usually means something in your life has reached a court date, or could soon — a charge, a summons, a bail hearing or a trial. You want someone who knows the courts in your area and can stand beside you in the Crown Court or magistrates' court. iComply is a free introduction service: you tell us what you need, and we introduce you to a suitable UK professional who quotes you directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a criminal barrister near me usually need
need_lead: Most people behind this search are facing a criminal matter and want representation that is close enough to their local courts to be practical.
needs: You have been charged with an offence and want a barrister to represent you at a bail hearing or first appearance.
You are due to stand trial in the Crown Court and want someone to present your case in front of the jury.
You are appearing in the magistrates' court and are unsure whether a barrister or a solicitor will handle your case.
You want to challenge a conviction or sentence and need a barrister to advise on an appeal.
You have been told your case may be suitable for a barrister instructed directly, and you want to know who is available near you.
context_heading: How criminal barristers are usually instructed
context: In the traditional route, your solicitor instructs the barrister for you, and the barrister works from chambers with clerks who manage diaries and fees. Legal aid often covers barrister fees in criminal matters, so it is worth asking about eligibility early. Private instructions are also possible, and some barristers registered under the Public Access scheme can be instructed directly by members of the public for suitable matters.

Barristers in England and Wales are regulated by the Bar Standards Board (BSB). You can check the Barristers' Register to see whether someone holds a current practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public. In Scotland the equivalent professionals are advocates, regulated through the Faculty of Advocates. iComply is not regulated and does not give legal advice — we simply make the introduction.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the offence or allegation you are facing, in your own words and as fully as you can.
Say which court your matter is in, or which court it is likely to be heard in, and the date if you have one.
Explain whether you already have a solicitor and whether they are instructing a barrister for you.
Mention whether you hope to use legal aid or expect to pay privately, without needing to give figures.
Say whether you want a barrister who can be instructed directly under the Public Access scheme.
Include the area you live in or can reasonably travel to, so the introduction is genuinely local to you.
questions: Are you able to accept instructions directly from me under the Public Access scheme, or would I need a solicitor to instruct you?
Do you hold a current practising certificate, and can you point me to your entry on the Barristers' Register?
Have you handled cases like mine in the court where my matter is being heard?
How do your fees work in a case like mine, and will you set them out before I commit?
Can you tell me whether legal aid is likely to be available for my situation?
Who will be my main point of contact at chambers, and how do I reach them?

faqs.q: Do I need a solicitor to instruct a criminal barrister?
faqs.a: Usually your solicitor instructs the barrister on your behalf, and the two work together on your case. Some barristers registered under the Public Access scheme can be instructed directly by members of the public for suitable matters, so it is worth asking.

faqs.q: Can legal aid cover a criminal barrister's fees?
faqs.a: Legal aid often covers barrister fees in criminal matters, and eligibility depends on your circumstances and the type of case. Ask the barrister or your solicitor about legal aid early so you understand where you stand.

faqs.q: How do I check that a barrister is properly regulated?
faqs.a: Barristers in England and Wales are regulated by the Bar Standards Board (BSB). You can check the Barristers' Register to see whether someone holds a current practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public.

faqs.q: What does price on application mean for a criminal barrister?
faqs.a: It means the barrister will quote you directly once they understand your case, rather than advertising a fixed figure. Ask for the quote in writing and check what it covers before you agree.
